details: Pripyat (Пр'ятть): Soviet nuclear city founded February 4 1970; purpose: housing for Chernobyl NPP workers and their families; designed as model Soviet city; population April 1986: 49,360 (official); average age: 26 years (youngest city in USSR); residents: ~16,000 children; NPP workers (~20,000); families; Soviet urban planning: standard 5-story Khrushchyovka blocks; modern (by Soviet standards) amusement park; cinema; supermarkets; sports complex; hospitals (Medchast 126); 3 swimming pools; Pripyat was awarded 'Model City' status by Ukrainian SSR in 1985; river: Pripyat River (3km to CEZ boundary); distance to Chernobyl NPP: 3.0 km NW
current_status_2026: Evacuation April 27 1986: announced by radio 13:10; 36 hours after explosion; 1200 buses; ~3 hours to evacuate 49,360 residents; told 'temporary' evacuation (3 days); residents left almost everything; pets left behind; Pripyat never repopulated; declared permanently abandoned 1990; category: ghost city; most photographed ghost city globally (pre-war ~60,000 tourists/year); UNESCO World Heritage nomination as cultural landscape 2022; HBO Chernobyl 2019: Pripyat filming location (Kharkiv Oblast served as substitute; Vilnius Lithuania for Pripyat interior shots); current access: day trips permitted with SNRIU permit; overnight prohibited; tourist infrastructure limited post-2022 war

details: Pripyat dose rate (April 2026; SaveEcoBot sensor): 4.932 µSv/hr; annual dose if permanently occupied: 4.932 × 8760 = 43.2 mSv/yr; occupational limit = 20 mSv/yr; public limit = 1 mSv/yr; therefore: Pripyat still not habitable (43× public limit); Cs-137 deposited in Pripyat vicinity: 600-3700 kBq/m² (near-field deposition from fuel particle and volatile aerosol NW plume); dose rate breakdown: external gamma from Cs-137 in soil dominant; internal pathway (mushrooms/berries/mushrooms from buildings) secondary; Pripyat comparison: Chernobyl city 0.209 µSv/hr (1.8 mSv/yr); background ~0.1-0.15 µSv/hr; Pripyat = 33-50× natural background = clearly elevated
current_status_2026: Trend: Cs-137 t½=30.17yr; 40yr elapsed = 1.33 half-lives; 60 km: 0.60 remaining; dose rate should be ~60% of 1987 level; but: soil fixation reduces external dose rate faster (as Cs-137 migrates deeper, gamma self-shielding increases); actual dose rate decline ~3-5%/yr; Pripyat dose rate 1987: estimated ~8-15 µSv/hr; 2026: 4.932 µSv/hr = 33-62% remaining; consistent with ~1.5-1.8 half-lives equivalent reduction (faster than radioactive decay alone due to soil migration and weathering); habitability timeline: public limit (1 mSv/yr = 0.114 µSv/hr) requires ~150yr additional decay → habitable ~2170-2200; see contamination_zones_REAL.csv

details: Hospital Medchast No. 126 (Медсанчастина №126): Pripyat city hospital; 3km from Chernobyl Unit 4; received first ARS patients April 26 1986 morning; had no experience with radiation casualties; Dr. Angelina Guskova was in Moscow (Hospital No. 6); local physicians: treated 26 first responders initially; diagnostic limitation: standard blood count equipment; no radiation specialist; no cytogenetics; treatment: gastric lavage; sedation; basic supportive care; first nuclear casualties in world history treated in a city hospital with no radiation medicine preparation; records: partially preserved; key observation: firefighters presenting with 'chemical' burns (beta burns to skin) that looked like sunburn + radiation sickness symptoms; 'metallic taste' = early ARS symptom
current_status_2026: Patient transfer: severe ARS patients stabilized at Medchast 126 → flown to Hospital No. 6 Moscow (Dr. Guskova); first transfer: April 26 afternoon and evening (13 firefighters + operators by first evening); total ARS patients Moscow: 134 by early May; Medchast 126 role: triage + stabilization only; hospital building: standing 2026; abandoned with all equipment 1986; some equipment still in place (radiation prevents removal); contaminated hospital = classic CEZ photography site; abandoned beds with patient linens; medical equipment; records partially survived; human remains story: patients' clothing abandoned in basement → still radioactive 2026; see chernobyl_first_responders_medical_REAL.csv

details: Pripyat amusement park: constructed 1985-1986; scheduled grand opening: May 1 1986 (May Day celebrations); actually opened briefly April 27 1986 (mayor ordered opening to give residents something to do while evacuation was being organized; theory: distraction from evacuation anxiety); May 1 opening = never happened; evacuation April 27; park used for <1 day; Ferris wheel (yellow-white; 26m diameter); bumper cars; rocket ride; all still standing 2026; Ferris wheel: contaminated (seat paint contains absorbed Cs-137 and hot particles); current dose rate near wheel: 2-5 µSv/hr; one of most photographed abandoned sites globally; yellow Ferris wheel = icon of Pripyat abandonment; appears in: Call of Duty video game; countless photojournalism pieces
current_status_2026: Pripyat cultural heritage: ghost city as preserved time capsule of 1986 Soviet life; unique historical value: (1) Soviet apartment living preserved; (2) Cold War nuclear technology narrative; (3) human displacement testimony; (4) nature reclamation laboratory; UNESCO nomination argument: 'exceptional testimony to an era' + 'universal significance' = meets World Heritage criteria; problem: active radiological hazard (dose rate) + ongoing decommissioning site + war conditions = UNESCO criteria against listing hazardous industrial sites; UK comparison: Orford Ness (UK nuclear test site) = National Nature Reserve but not UNESCO WH; challenge: preservation vs radiological safety

details: Chernobyl city (town): 14km S of ChNPP; evacuated 1986 (13,716 residents); declared partially accessible for workers post-1986; current residents: ~1000 SSE CHNPP workers on rotation basis (not permanent residents); also: State Agency of Ukraine for Exclusion Zone Management (DAZV) employees; border guard; police; not permanently inhabited; workers: 2-week rotations; dormitory accommodation; food brought from outside CEZ; recreational facilities limited; dose rate: 0.209 µSv/hr (April 2026 SaveEcoBot); annual dose if permanently occupied: 1.8 mSv/yr; above public limit (1 mSv/yr) but habitable for occupational workers (20 mSv/yr limit); Chernobyl city shops: souvenir shops for tourists; small cafes
current_status_2026: Chernobyl city vs Pripyat: Chernobyl city is 14km from NPP vs 3km for Pripyat; lower initial deposition (volatile aerosol plume was NW toward Pripyat; Cs-137 at Chernobyl city: 150-600 kBq/m²); 0.209 vs 4.932 µSv/hr = factor 24 lower dose rate; approaching habitability threshold: 0.209 µSv/hr × 8760 = 1.83 mSv/yr; only 1.83× above public limit; with soil remediation (removing top 5cm): could reduce by ~50%; Chernobyl city = most likely candidate for limited resettlement in future if dose rates continue declining at ~3-5%/yr; public limit (0.114 µSv/hr) reached in ~15-20yr

details: Red Forest: 10 km² of pine forest immediately W of ChNPP; named for reddish-brown color as trees died from beta/gamma doses > 50 mGy/day in 1986; dead trees bulldozed and buried in shallow trenches 1986 (later found to create groundwater contamination); birch and aspen naturally regenerated; second-generation forest = evolved/selected for radiation tolerance; current dose rate: 2-10+ µSv/hr average; hotspots: up to 100+ µSv/hr near original tree burial trenches; Red Forest contains: highest density of burial trenches for contaminated material; vehicle storage; tree debris; estimated residual Cs-137: mean 412,000 Bq/kg soil; area = most contaminated surface soil in CEZ after NPP immediate vicinity
current_status_2026: 2022 Russian military impact: Russian forces dug trenches directly through Red Forest area (preparing defensive positions); IAEA post-withdrawal inspection: found no significant additional contamination plume to aquifer from trenching; localized soil disturbance; dose to soldiers digging: estimated 10-50 mSv/day for those working in trench-digging; some soldiers reportedly developed ARS-like symptoms; however: military doctor chain of custody unclear; no independent verification; 2020 wildfire: 11,500 hectares burned including Red Forest areas; post-fire soil erosion increased lateral transport; see red_forest_waste_sites_REAL.csv

details: Chernobyl NPP site (April 2026): Units 1-3: in 'safe confinement' conversion process; defueling complete (all fuel removed from Units 1-3 to ISF-1 and ISF-2); decommissioning Phase 1 (2001-2028): radiological characterization; hazardous substance identification; decommissioning documentation; Unit 4: under New Safe Confinement (NSC); corium stable; flux measurements ongoing; NSC: Feb 2025 drone strike repaired (outer cladding); inner arch intact; ISF-2: ~30% loaded (6,000+ of 21,217 assemblies); loading ongoing; target completion 2028; ISF-1: wet pools holding remaining assemblies; active cooling required; Solid Radioactive Waste Treatment (SRWT) facility: operating; Chernobyl NPP staff (SSE CHNPP): ~2,500 employees total
current_status_2026: Post-2022 recovery: site fully back under Ukrainian control since March 31 2022; SSE CHNPP management restored; IAEA permanent on-site presence from May 2022; international decommissioning assistance resumed (EU; G7; US); NSC repair funded; ISF-2 loading resumed; SNRIU regulatory oversight restored; 2025-2028 priority: complete ISF-2 loading (passive safety priority); begin Unit 1-3 decommissioning Phase 2 planning; NSC cladding repair; uranium/plutonium inventory verification; potential for international tourists when security situation allows

details: Self-settlers (Самосели / Samosely): Ukrainians who returned to live illegally in Zone of Alienation after evacuation; peak: late 1980s ~1200 persons; current (2026): ~200-300 (declining with age; most elderly); demographics: predominantly elderly women (60-80+yr); rural communities; attachment to homeland/ancestral land; accept radiation risk for: ability to die at home; maintain traditional lifestyle; tend graves of family; engage in subsistence farming; locations: villages of Chernobyl, Sukachi, Parishiv, Opachychi and ~10 others within CEZ; recognized by Ukrainian government since 1990s (utilities partially maintained; occasional ambulance service)
current_status_2026: Self-settler radiation exposure: external gamma dose ~2-5 mSv/yr (well below occupational limit); dietary Cs-137: from mushrooms/berries/garden vegetables/forest game = 10-100 Bq/kg typically; WBC monitoring: carried out by Ukrainian scientists; body burdens declining with age and declining soil contamination; main risk pathway: food production within CEZ (especially mushrooms with Fv=0.03-16.7); Prussian Blue prescription offered but not always accepted; self-settler lifespan: appears NOT shorter than age-matched non-displaced Ukrainian populations (WHO 2005; Johnson 2021); possible explanation: psychological benefit of home attachment offsets small radiation increase; see cez_management_regulations_REAL.csv; chernobyl_social_displacement_REAL.csv
